provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Reviewing New York's permanent-neglect scheme, the Supreme Court held that the fair-preponderance standard then prescribed by Family Court Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause and that a State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before irrevocably severing parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: This New York-origin decision fixes the constitutional burden of proof for every termination of parental rights.
key_cases.quote: the "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard prescribed by Fam. Ct. Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of parental rights for permanent neglect, holding that the agency must first prove diligent efforts and that the parent failed to maintain contact with or plan for the child for more than a year, and that at the separate dispositional hearing the child's best interests control with no presumption favoring return to the parent.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading New York statement of the permanent-neglect elements and of the two-stage fact-finding then best-interests structure of a termination trial.
key_cases.quote: the threshold inquiry by the court in any neglect proceeding must be whether the agency exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parental relationship

key_cases.holding: The Court held that an agency seeking termination for permanent neglect must affirmatively plead in detail and prove by clear and convincing evidence that it exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parent-child relationship, and that failure to carry that threshold burden requires dismissal of the petition as to that parent.
key_cases.relevance: Diligent efforts are a necessary prerequisite, pleaded in detail and proved by clear and convincing evidence, to any permanent-neglect finding.
key_cases.quote: It has declared as a matter of public policy that the State may not intervene to terminate a parent's rights when assistance in strengthening the family has not been forthcoming

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed terminations of the parental rights of incarcerated fathers, holding that although incarceration alone is not a ground for termination and the parent's special circumstances must be considered, a plan consisting only of indefinite long-term foster care for the duration of the child's minority does not satisfy the statutory planning requirement.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling New York authority on permanent neglect and termination where the parent is incarcerated.
key_cases.quote: an incarcerated parent may not satisfy the planning requirement of the statute where the only plan offered is long-term foster care lasting potentially for the child's entire minority

key_cases.holding: The Court held that awarding custody to foster parents under Social Services Law § 392(6) was impermissible and that the best-interests inquiry for a child in temporary foster care compares continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent or other relative or suitable person, rather than measuring parent against foster parent.
key_cases.relevance: Termination requires clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground, and a suspended judgment gives a strictly time-limited second chance.
key_cases.quote: analysis of the child's "best interest" must begin not by measuring biological parent against foster parent but by weighing past and continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination order, holding for the first time that the right to assigned counsel in proceedings to terminate parental rights necessarily includes the right to effective assistance, and that counsel who had never spoken with the parent before the fact-finding hearing and announced he would remain silent did not provide it.
key_cases.relevance: A termination entered after constitutionally ineffective representation cannot stand and must be reversed.
key_cases.quote: the right to assigned counsel in proceedings to terminate parental rights necessarily encompasses the right to effective assistance of counsel

timeline_requirements.deadline: Initial hearing commenced within 6 months; each later hearing no later than 6 months from completion of the previous one
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Sixty days after the child was removed from the home (later hearings run from completion of the previous permanency hearing)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.Y. Fam. Ct. Act § 1089(a)
Must file TPR or document compelling reason

notice_requirements.timing: No later than 14 days before the date certain for the permanency hearing
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in N.Y. Fam. Ct. Act § 1089(b)
